title: Level 3 · Python Data Structures
blurb: Store and organise data with strings, lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries.

lessons.title: Strings (indexing, slicing, methods)
lessons.concept: A string is text, and every character has a position (an index) starting at 0; negative indexes count from the end, so word[-1] is the last letter. Slicing takes a piece: word[0:3] gives the first three characters. Methods like .upper(), .lower() and .strip() return new text.
lessons.why: Usernames, emails, messages and file names are all strings that programs cut up and clean.
lessons.example_note: Prints the first and last letters, the first three letters and the uppercase name.
lessons.prompt: Write a function short_code(name) that returns the first 3 letters of name in uppercase, followed by the length of the name. Example: short_code('Chennai') returns 'CHE7'.
hints: name[:3] gives the first three characters.
Join text and a number with str(len(name)).

lessons.title: Lists
lessons.concept: A list stores many values in order, inside square brackets: marks = [80, 65, 90]. Use indexes like strings (marks[0], marks[-1]), len(marks) for the size, and you can change an item with marks[1] = 70.
lessons.why: Carts, student lists and search results are all lists.
lessons.example:
marks = [80, 65, 90]
print(marks[0], marks[-1])
marks[1] = 70
print(marks, len(marks))
lessons.example_note: Reads the first and last item, changes the middle one and shows the list and its length.
lessons.prompt: Write a function first_last(items) that returns a new list holding the first and the last item of items. Example: first_last(['a', 'b', 'c']) returns ['a', 'c'].

lessons.title: List Methods (append, extend, insert, pop, remove)
lessons.concept: append(x) adds one item at the end, extend(list) adds many, insert(i, x) adds at position i, pop() removes (and returns) the last item, and remove(x) deletes the first item equal to x.
lessons.why: A shopping cart grows and shrinks all the time as people add and remove products.
lessons.example:
cart = ['rice']
cart.append('milk')
cart.extend(['eggs', 'tea'])
cart.insert(0, 'oil')
cart.pop()
cart.remove('rice')
print(cart)
lessons.example_note: Builds and trims a cart; prints ['oil', 'milk', 'eggs'].
lessons.prompt: Write edit_cart(first). Start with cart = [first, 'sugar', 'oil'], then in this order: append 'milk', extend with ['eggs', 'tea'], insert 'salt' at position 1, pop the last item, and remove 'sugar'. Return the cart.
lessons.starter:
def edit_cart(first):
    cart = [first, 'sugar', 'oil']
    # append, extend, insert, pop, remove
    return cart
lessons.solution:
def edit_cart(first):
    cart = [first, 'sugar', 'oil']
    cart.append('milk')
    cart.extend(['eggs', 'tea'])
    cart.insert(1, 'salt')
    cart.pop()
    cart.remove('sugar')
    return cart
hints: Each method is called on the list: cart.append('milk').
Order: append, extend, insert(1, 'salt'), pop(), remove('sugar').

lessons.title: Tuples
lessons.concept: A tuple is like a list but cannot be changed after it is created. It is written with round brackets: point = (3, 4). Indexing and len() work as with lists, and a function can return several values as a tuple.
lessons.why: Fixed groups such as coordinates, RGB colours or a (min, max) pair are perfect tuples.
lessons.example_note: Reads the two values of a tuple and its length.
lessons.prompt: Write a function min_max(marks) that takes a list or tuple of numbers and returns a tuple (lowest, highest). Example: min_max([40, 90, 65]) returns (40, 90).
hints: Python has built-in min() and max().
Return two values separated by a comma.

lessons.title: Sets
lessons.concept: A set is an unordered collection of unique items, written with curly brackets: {1, 2, 3}. Duplicates vanish automatically. Make one from a list with set(items); in checks are very fast.
lessons.why: Removing duplicate email addresses or counting distinct visitors is a job for sets.
lessons.example:
names = ['Asha', 'Ravi', 'Asha', 'Mei']
unique = set(names)
print(len(unique))
print('Ravi' in unique)
lessons.example_note: Three unique names remain out of four, and Ravi is in the set.
lessons.prompt: Write unique_visitors(names) that removes duplicates using a set and returns the unique names as a sorted list. Example: unique_visitors(['b', 'a', 'b']) returns ['a', 'b'].
hints: Sets have no order, so use sorted() to get a list.

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.concept: A dictionary stores key: value pairs in curly brackets: student = {'name': 'Asha', 'age': 20}. Look up a value with its key, student['name'], and add or change one with student['city'] = 'Pune'.
lessons.why: Records such as a user profile, a product with its price or a student with marks are dictionaries.
lessons.example_note: Reads one value, adds a new pair and prints the dictionary.
lessons.prompt: Write make_student(name, marks) that returns a dictionary with the keys 'name', 'marks' and 'passed' (in that order); passed is True when marks is 40 or more.
lessons.solution:
def make_student(name, marks):
    return {'name': name, 'marks': marks, 'passed': marks >= 40}
hints: Write the dictionary with curly brackets and key: value pairs.

lessons.title: Dictionary Methods (keys, values, items, get, update)
lessons.concept: d.keys() lists the keys, d.values() the values and d.items() the (key, value) pairs. d.get(key, default) looks up safely without an error if the key is missing, and d.update({...}) adds or changes several pairs at once.
lessons.why: Inventory systems, word counters and settings screens all lean on these methods.
lessons.example:
stock = {'pen': 3, 'book': 8}
stock.update({'ink': 5})
print(list(stock.keys()))
print(sum(stock.values()))
print(stock.get('bag', 0))
for name, qty in stock.items():
    print(name, qty)
lessons.example_note: Updates the stock then reads keys, values, a safe lookup and the pairs.
lessons.prompt: Write summary(stock), where stock maps item names to quantities. First update it with {'pen': 50}. Then return a dictionary with these keys in order: 'names' (sorted list of keys()), 'total' (sum of values()), 'ink' (get of 'ink' with default 0) and 'low' (sorted list of item names whose quantity is below 5, found by looping over items()).
hints: for name, qty in stock.items(): lets you check each quantity.
Build low with append, then return the dictionary with sorted(stock.keys()), sum(stock.values()), stock.get('ink', 0), sorted(low).

lessons.title: Nested Lists
lessons.concept: A list can hold other lists. This makes a table: table = [[80, 70], [60, 90]]. table[1] is the second row and table[1][0] is the first number in that row. Loop over the rows to process each one.
lessons.why: Marks sheets, game boards and spreadsheets are lists of rows.
lessons.example:
table = [[80, 70], [60, 90]]
print(table[1])
print(table[1][0])
for row in table:
    print(sum(row))
lessons.example_note: Reads a row, one cell, and the sum of each row.
lessons.prompt: Each row of table holds one student's marks in several subjects. Write row_totals(table) that returns a list with the total of each row. Example: row_totals([[80, 70], [60, 90]]) returns [150, 150].
lessons.starter:

lessons.title: Nested Dictionaries
lessons.concept: A dictionary value can be another dictionary. Chain the keys to reach inside: student['marks']['maths']. This keeps related details grouped together.
lessons.why: Data from websites and apps (JSON) is mostly dictionaries inside dictionaries.
lessons.example_note: Reads one inner value and the total of the inner dictionary.
lessons.prompt: Write total_marks(student). student looks like {'name': 'Asha', 'marks': {'maths': 90, 'science': 80}}. Return the sum of all the values in its 'marks' dictionary.
hints: First reach the inner dictionary with student['marks'].

lessons.title: Mutable vs Immutable
lessons.concept: Mutable objects (lists, dictionaries, sets) can be changed in place. Immutable objects (numbers, strings, tuples) cannot. If you write b = a for a list, both names share one list, so a change through b also changes a. Use a.copy() to get an independent list.
lessons.why: Many bugs come from changing a list that another part of the program is still using.
lessons.example:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)
c = a.copy()
c.append(4)
print(a, c)
lessons.example_note: a changes through b, but not through the copy c.
lessons.prompt: Write with_bonus(marks) that returns a new list in which every mark is increased by 5, without changing the original list. Start with result = marks.copy().
lessons.starter:
def with_bonus(marks):
    result = marks.copy()
    # add 5 to every item of result
    return result
hints: result[i] += 5 updates one position; loop over range(len(result)).

lessons.title: Unpacking (list, tuple, dict)
lessons.concept: Unpacking spreads a collection into separate names: name, age = ('Asha', 20) works for tuples and lists, and first, *rest = [1, 2, 3] gathers the leftovers. With ** you unpack a dictionary's pairs into another dictionary: {**a, **b} merges them.
lessons.why: It makes code shorter and clearer when functions return several values or when you merge settings and records.
lessons.example_note: Unpacks a tuple and a list, then merges a dictionary into a new one.
lessons.prompt: Write make_card(person, contact). person is a tuple (name, age) and contact is a dictionary. Unpack the tuple into name and age, then return a dictionary with 'name', 'age' followed by all the pairs of contact (unpack it with **).
hints: name, age = person unpacks the tuple.
Inside the new dictionary, **contact copies every pair of contact.
